body: The school does not say “over fifteen thousand books”. It says **17,574**, alongside **25 periodicals** — a figure with a units digit on it, which means somebody counted rather than rounded.

The periodicals are the quieter half and the more useful one. A library of books alone is a place you go for something you were already sent to find; a shelf of periodicals is where a reader meets a subject nobody assigned them.
And the photograph is the argument. The room is not empty in it: long tables, a full class reading, and a member of staff at the head of the row.

round.kicker: What is run around the collection
round.heading:
A carnival,
{{and a club with racks.}}
body: The school runs a **Reading Carnival** — a book fair set up along its own corridors rather than in a hall, so classes file past it on the way to lessons. Its racks are signed by section, and the signage names something the site had not recorded: a **Reading Club**, with racks headed *Study Skills*, *Storybook* and *New Release*.
Alongside it the school gives an **Ardent Reader Award** to its most committed readers, published in seventy-five photographs — though not, notably, with the winners’ names, so none is given here.

lab.kicker: The half a book cannot do
lab.heading:
Recorded,
{{then reviewed.}}
body: Reading is the input. The school’s **language laboratory** — one of its twelve laboratories — exists for the output, and its description is precise about what makes it different: *spoken language, practised aloud and recorded, which is the part a textbook cannot do.*

The recording is the whole point. A student who has only ever been corrected in the moment has never heard themselves; a student who has been recorded has, and that is a different kind of learning from reading a page about pronunciation.
Above: the school assembled for the Ardent Reader Award. The school has published no photograph of the language laboratory itself.

stage.kicker: And where the speaking ends up
stage.heading:
On a platform,
{{from Class I.}}
body: The test of a language programme is not the room — it is whether children are put in front of an audience, and how early. Sunbeam’s published record answers both, and the first answer is Class I.
